extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary); patent practitioners and applicants (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis when evaluating whether a claim reciting a nature-based product is a product-of-nature exception under the patent eligibility framework (Step 2A / Prong One and Prong Two). Covers when to apply the analysis, how to pick counterparts, what characteristics to compare, and how to evaluate marked differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claimed nature-based product has markedly different characteristics → not a product-of-nature exception (Step 2A: NO)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that has markedly different characteristics, then the claim does not recite a product of nature exception and is eligible (Step 2A: NO) at Pathway B unless the claim recites another exception (such as a law of nature or abstract idea, or a different natural phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For claims where the entire claim is a single nature-based product (e.g., a claim to "a Lactobacillus bacterium"), once a markedly different characteristic in that product is shown, no further analysis would be necessary for eligibility because no product of nature exception is recited (i.e., Step 2B is not necessary because the answer to Step 2A is NO). For claims including additional limitations, examiners should still consider whether the claim recites another exception that requires further eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: If claimed nature-based product lacks markedly different characteristics → product-of-nature exception (requires further analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim includes a nature-based product that does not exhibit markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state, then the claim recites a 'product of nature' exception, and requires further analysis in Step 2A Prong Two to determine whether the claim as a whole integrates the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that a limitation is a product-of-nature exception does not end analysis; examiners must proceed to Prong Two (and Step 2B if necessary) to determine whether additional claim elements integrate the exception into a patent-eligible application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the markedly different characteristics analysis only to nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied only to the nature-based product limitations in the claim to determine whether the nature-based products are 'product of nature' exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not overly extend the analysis to claim elements that, when viewed as a whole, are not nature-based. Analyze only the specific nature-based product limitations (whether standalone or as part of a combination) rather than unrelated claim elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No analysis needed for limitations that are naturally occurring
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature-based product limitation is naturally occurring, there is no need to perform the markedly different characteristics analysis because the limitation is by definition directed to a naturally occurring product and thus falls under the product of nature exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product limitation is not naturally occurring (for example due to human intervention), then the markedly different characteristics analysis must be performed to determine whether the claimed product limitation is a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product claims: apply analysis to the entire claimed product or the resultant nature-based combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the claim is to a nature-based product by itself (e.g., a claim to "a Lactobacillus bacterium"), the markedly different characteristics analysis should be applied to the entire product. Where the claim is to a nature-based product produced by combining multiple components (e.g., "a probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk"), the analysis should be applied to the resultant nature-based combination rather than its component parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim is to a nature-based product combined with non-nature elements (e.g., a 'yogurt starter kit' comprising Lactobacillus plus container and instructions), apply the markedly different analysis only to the nature-based product limitation (Lactobacillus). Non-nature elements are not subject to this analysis but may be evaluated in Prong Two/Step 2B if the nature-based product is found to be an exception. Case examples: Chakrabarty (entire bacterium), Funk Bros. (analyze bacterial mixture).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims: focus on whether the claimed product has markedly different characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: For a product-by-process claim (e.g., a cloned farm animal produced by nuclear transfer cloning), the analysis turns on whether the nature-based product in the claim has markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2113 for more on product-by-process claims. The fact that a product is claimed by its process does not change that the substantive question is whether the product itself is markedly different from its natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims: generally focus on active steps; only apply MD analysis when claim is in substance a product claim
rubrics_metrics.description: For a process claim, the general rule is that the claim is not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for nature-based products used in the process, because process analysis should focus on the active steps of the process rather than the products used in those steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: where a process claim reciting a nature-based product is drafted such that there is no difference in substance from a product claim (e.g., 'a method of providing an apple'), then the claim is subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis for the recited nature-based product. Case examples: Rapid Litig. Mgmt. v. CellzDirect; Ariosa Diagnostics (detecting cffDNA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step framework for performing the markedly different characteristics analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis involves (a) selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s) to the nature-based product limitation, (b) identifying appropriate characteristics for analysis, and (c) evaluating characteristics to determine whether they are 'markedly different'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each step should be carried out on a case-by-case basis, using the claim language and the closest naturally occurring counterpart(s) in their natural state. The analysis looks at structure, function, and/or other properties as recited or encompassed by the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting the appropriate naturally occurring counterpart(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state, the first step in the analysis is to select the appropriate counterpart(s) to the nature-based product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the nature-based product is derived from a naturally occurring thing, the counterpart is that natural thing (e.g., deoxyacid A compared to acid A). Do not confuse the counterpart with other material that may occur naturally with or adjacent to it (e.g., an isolated gene is compared to the gene, not the entire chromosome). When multiple possible counterparts exist, compare to the closest naturally occurring counterpart (examiner may use art expertise to select). For combinations with no natural counterpart, compare components individually. Best practice: identify the selected counterpart in the Office action when rejecting as ineligible to clarify the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate characteristics for comparison must be possessed by the claimed product
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate characteristics must be possessed by the claimed product, because it is the claim that must define the invention to be patented. Unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute to eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners identify characteristics from what is recited in the claim and what is encompassed within the broadest reasonable interpretation. Characteristics may be explicitly recited (e.g., chemical name indicating structural differences) or inferred from the BRI (e.g., 'isolated gene B' implies sequence and encoded protein). Case citation: Roslin (unclaimed characteristics cannot contribute).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of characteristics to consider: structure, function, and other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Markedly different characteristics can be expressed as the product's structure, function, and/or other properties, and are evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-limiting categories and examples courts have considered include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities (e.g., protein-encoding information; binding abilities; infectivity; biodegradation; therapeutic effects), chemical and physical properties (e.g., alkalinity, ductility), phenotypic characteristics (shape, size, color, behavior), and structure and form (physical presence of plasmids, chemical/crystalline form, nucleotide sequence, genotype). Specific judicial examples are provided in the guidance (Myriad, Ambry, Chakrabarty, Parke-Davis, Marden, Roslin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating whether a characteristic is 'markedly different' (must be changed, not innate or incidental, and attributable to applicant)
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a marked difference, a characteristic must be changed as compared to nature, and cannot be an inherent or innate characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart or an incidental change in a characteristic of the naturally occurring counterpart. Applicant must have caused the claimed product to possess at least one characteristic that is different from that of the counterpart.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no change in any characteristic, the claimed product lacks markedly different characteristics and is a product-of-nature exception. If there is a change in at least one characteristic and the change came about or was produced by applicant's efforts or influences, then the change will generally be considered a markedly different characteristic such that the claimed product is not a product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to have markedly different characteristics (illustrative case guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chakrabarty: genetically modified bacterium with additional plasmids and the ability to degrade multiple hydrocarbons was markedly different and eligible. Myriad: cDNA (exons only) was structurally different from genomic DNA and was not a product of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these cases as exemplars: Chakrabarty demonstrates combination of changed structure (additional plasmids) and changed function (degrading multiple hydrocarbons). Myriad shows structural change (exon-only cDNA) can suffice even if functional characteristics (protein encoded) remain the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of products found to lack markedly different characteristics (illustrative case guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad (isolated genomic DNA), Ambry (primers), Marden (ductile vanadium), and Roslin (cloned animals) illustrate situations where claimed products lacked markedly different characteristics because changes were incidental, innate, or unclaimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Myriad: isolation alone (removal from chromosome) was incidental and not a marked difference. Ambry: primers had the same nucleotide sequence and innate binding function as natural DNA. Roslin: clones maintained donor DNA and claimed phenotypic differences were not claimed and therefore could not establish marked difference. Marden: inherent material property (ductility) is not a marked difference if not created by combination or chemical change.
